title: How LLMs Actually Work

character.name: The Wordsmith
character.tagline: I'm just guessing the next word. Extremely well. Billions of times.

oneLiner: Under the hood of ChatGPT & friends: tokens, embeddings, next-token prediction, and the context window.
analogy: An LLM is the world's most well-read autocomplete. It chops your text into puzzle pieces called tokens, turns each into a bundle of numbers (an embedding) that captures meaning, then predicts the next most likely token — over and over — to build a reply. It has no live memory between chats; each turn it re-reads the whole conversation that fits inside its context window (its short-term desk space). 'Temperature' is how adventurous its guesses are: low = safe and repetitive, high = creative and occasionally unhinged.
objectives: Understand tokenization and why models see tokens, not letters or words.
Grasp next-token prediction as the core mechanism.
Understand the context window and its limits.
Know what temperature and sampling do to outputs, and why hallucinations happen.
keyConcepts: Text is split into tokens (word-pieces); the model reads and generates token by token.
An LLM predicts the probability of the next token given all previous tokens, then samples one and repeats.
The context window is the maximum amount of text (tokens) the model can consider at once — its working memory for that request.
LLMs are stateless between calls: they only 'remember' what you resend in the prompt/context.
Temperature and top-p control randomness: low is focused/deterministic, high is more creative/varied.
Hallucinations occur because the model predicts plausible-sounding text, not verified facts — it optimizes for likely, not true.

keyTerms.plain: A chunk of text (often a word-piece). The model's Lego brick.
Guess the next brick, again and again, to build a sentence.
How much text the model can hold on its desk at once.
The creativity dial: low = safe, high = wild.
Confidently making stuff up that sounds right but isn't.

scenarios.scenario: A user complains that the chatbot 'forgot' something they said 50 messages ago in a very long conversation.
scenarios.question: What's the most likely technical explanation?

options.label: Older messages fell outside the model's context window, so it no longer sees them
The model has a personal grudge
The GPU deleted the memory to save power
LLMs permanently store every conversation by default

scenarios.explanation: LLMs only consider what fits in the context window. In long chats, earlier content can be truncated/summarized out, so the model effectively 'forgets' it unless it's resupplied.

scenarios.scenario: You need highly consistent, repeatable output from an LLM for a data-extraction task.
scenarios.question: Which setting helps most?

options.label: A low temperature (near 0) for focused, deterministic responses
A very high temperature for creativity

scenarios.explanation: Low temperature makes the model pick high-probability tokens consistently, yielding more repeatable, deterministic output — ideal for extraction/formatting tasks.

quiz.question: At its core, an LLM generates text by:
options: Looking up answers in a database
Repeatedly predicting the next token given the preceding tokens
quiz.answer: Repeatedly predicting the next token given the preceding tokens
quiz.explanation: LLMs are next-token predictors: they estimate the probability of the next token and sample one, again and again, to produce text.

quiz.question: What is the 'context window'?
options: The maximum amount of text (tokens) the model can consider in a single request
quiz.answer: The maximum amount of text (tokens) the model can consider in a single request
quiz.explanation: The context window bounds how much input+output the model can handle at once; content beyond it isn't seen.

quiz.question: Why do LLMs hallucinate?
options: They are connected to a lie database
They generate statistically plausible text, which isn't always factually correct
They run out of GPU memory
quiz.answer: They generate statistically plausible text, which isn't always factually correct
quiz.explanation: LLMs optimize for likely-sounding continuations, not verified truth, so they can produce confident but false statements.

quiz.question: Increasing 'temperature' generally makes outputs:
quiz.explanation: Higher temperature flattens the probability distribution, increasing variety and creativity (and risk of incoherence); lower temperature is more focused.

quiz.question: Between separate API calls, a standard LLM:
options: Is stateless — it only 'knows' what you include in the prompt/context
Stores your data in its weights instantly
quiz.answer: Is stateless — it only 'knows' what you include in the prompt/context
quiz.explanation: Models don't retain memory across calls by default; conversation history must be resent within the context window.
